title: Nanak's twelve months
hookLine: Guru Nanak's own twelve months, older and more stark than Guru Arjan's (Tukhari, ang 1107)

cards: What month is it? The quick answer comes off a phone: a name, a number, a box on a grid. But the Punjab has an older way of naming time, months called Chet and Vaisakh, Savan and Poh, each with its own weather.

Guru Nanak wrote a poem through that calendar, a Barah Maha: twelve months of a soul missing its Beloved. You met it once on this path, in a single glance. Over the next few days, it goes season by season.
Today, before a single flower opens: how it begins.

teach.b: The poem sits in Raga Tukhari, on ang eleven hundred seven of the Guru Granth Sahib, under Guru Nanak's name. First, the frame. It doesn't start with spring.
It starts with a word to the listener. In plain English, not word for word: hear this. Each one lives out the deeds done before.
On every head comes joy or sorrow, and whatever You give is good. Then the bride speaks. This world is Yours, Lord, so what is my state?
Without You I can't live even a moment. Before any month is named, you know who's speaking and what she lacks, and every season is seen through that lack. Second, the sound.
Each month gets its own long, unhurried stanza, piling up blossoms, bees, a blazing sun, lightning, frost, then turning again to the same ache: the Beloved is not home. Third, the voice.
The Granth holds another Barah Maha, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh, which this path read in year two. Both are true to the same longing.
Some readers find Nanak's the starker of the two: heavier weather, a rawer cry, comfort held back until late. Put simply, it's a year where little changes outside while everything inside waits.
Spring, the heat, the rains, the cold: each gets its turn.

how: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha is sung in kirtan in Raga Tukhari and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

s: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha opens with the flowers of spring
it opens with a call to listen, and the bride saying she can't live a moment without the Lord.
the Granth holds a second Barah Maha, by Guru Arjan
Guru Arjan's is in Raga Majh; Nanak's is in Raga Tukhari.
in the poem, every month brings a new longing for something different
the weather changes, but the ache is the same: the Beloved is not home.

games.q: you're about to sing twelve months of longing. how does Guru Nanak's poem begin?
o: with a call to listen, and a word on deeds and what God gives.
games.why: it opens with 'listen': each lives out past deeds, joy or sorrow comes, and whatever You give is good. only then do the months begin.

practice: Say the name of the month you're in, quietly, the Punjabi one if you know it, or the one you use.
Let your breath slow and notice what this month has brought: the light at the window, the air on your skin, what's growing or falling outside.
Then name, gently, what you're waiting for this month, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.

wordCard.voice: Nanak's twelve months. Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in Raga Tukhari, which opens by asking us to listen, then walks the year through a bride's longing. Today's word.

orig.note: barah maha: twelve months, the heading over Guru Nanak's poem in Tukhari.

carryVoice: Your line: nanak's months. A whole year of weather, read as one long love. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Tukhari, Mahala 1, Barah Maha, opening stanza, Ang 1107 (listen; deeds done before; joy or sorrow; what You give is good; without You I can't live a moment)
